lead: This unit moves from Hyperledger Fabric to the places blockchains are used: finance, supply chains, health, agriculture, IoT, smart cities, the metaverse and enterprise AI. After it you can explain how chaincode runs, compare Ripple, Quorum, Tendermint, Kadena and Rootstock, and judge scalability and privacy claims.
about: The unit starts with Hyperledger frameworks and the Fabric model (6.1), then chaincode as Fabric’s smart contract (6.2). Chapters 6.3 to 6.5 apply the same shared-ledger idea to finance and insurance, supply chain and logistics, and health, agriculture, IoT and smart cities. Chapter 6.6 looks at the metaverse value chain; 6.7 compares Ripple, Quorum, Tendermint, Kadena and Rootstock. Chapter 6.8 faces scalability, privacy and other limits, and 6.9 joins enterprise blockchain with AI. Each chapter uses earlier units on hashing, consensus and Ethereum only as needed, so the thread is: platform, contract, application, new platform, limit, enterprise.

chapters.idea: Hyperledger is a family of permissioned blockchain frameworks, and Fabric runs a channel as a set of peers, orderers and identities with an endorsement policy.
chapters.depth: Cover Hyperledger frameworks (Fabric, Sawtooth, Indy, Besu, Iroha), tools (Explorer, Caliper), and building blocks: ledger, membership, consensus, chaincode, events. Explain Fabric model: organisations, peers, orderers, channels, MSP identities, endorsement, ordering, commit, private data. Keep consensus algorithms as names only. Some syllabi call the building blocks 'components'.

figure.title: Fabric transaction flow
figure.aria: A client sends a proposal to two peers, both endorse, the orderer orders a block, a committer validates it, and the channel ledger is written.
figure.caption: A Fabric transaction collects endorsements from the peers named by the policy, is ordered, then committed to the channel ledger.

chapters.example: Org A has 2 peers (A1, A2) and Org B has 2 peers (B1, B2); one orderer serves the channel. The endorsement policy needs one peer from Org A and one from Org B. A proposal is endorsed by A1, A2 and B1. How many distinct organisations endorsed? Does it satisfy the policy? Answer: two organisations, A and B; yes, because A1 (or A2) and B1 satisfy the AND policy. The extra A2 signature is allowed but not required.
chapters.trap: Confusing the orderer with a miner; a Fabric orderer orders transactions, it does not execute chaincode or mine.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 private and consortium blockchain types; Unit 3 transaction life cycle.
chapters.leave: Consensus proofs, hashing internals and Bitcoin mining to Unit 3 and Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Chaincode is Fabric's smart contract; it runs in a container, reads and writes channel state, and only commits if the endorsement policy is met.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover chaincode lifecycle: package, install, approve, commit, invoke, query; namespaces; endorsement policies; private data collections; chaincode in Go, Java and Node.js; SHIM API; deterministic execution. Distinguish chaincode from Solidity contracts. Some syllabi call chaincode 'smart contract' in Hyperledger.

figure.aria: A client proposes a transfer, a peer returns an endorsed read-write set, the orderer sends a block, a committing peer validates and writes, and the client queries the new owner.
figure.caption: Chaincode execution is simulated at endorsement, but the state changes only after ordering and commit.

chapters.example: Chaincode asset CAR1 has owner Asha and price ₹5,00,000. Invoke TransferAsset(CAR1, Ravi) needs endorsements from Org A and Org B. Both peers endorse. The orderer includes the transaction in a block. At commit, the policy is checked and owner becomes Ravi. QueryAsset(CAR1) then returns Ravi. If only Org A endorses, the transaction is invalid at commit.
chapters.trap: Thinking chaincode execution changes the ledger immediately; it changes only after ordering and commit, and only if the endorsement policy passes.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1; Unit 5 smart-contract concept and token transfers.
chapters.leave: Solidity, the EVM, and consensus algorithms to Unit 5 and Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Finance and insurance use blockchains to share one tamper-evident record of payments, trade documents and claims among parties that do not fully trust each other.
chapters.depth: Cover cross-border payments, trade finance, letter of credit, KYC, tokenised assets, bond settlement, insurance policy and claims, parametric insurance, reinsurance. Explain smart-contract payout conditions and shared audit. Keep Bitcoin payment mechanics to Unit 4. Some syllabi group this as 'blockchain in finance'.

figure.title: Insurance claim on a shared ledger
figure.aria: A policy is recorded on-chain, a claim event arrives, a smart contract checks the deductible, a payout is made, and an audit log keeps the history.
figure.caption: The smart contract applies policy rules to a claim, but off-chain events still need trusted data or an oracle.

chapters.example: A health policy has sum insured ₹5,00,000 and a deductible of ₹10,000. The hospital submits a claim of ₹1,20,000. The smart contract checks that the policy is active and the claim is below the sum insured. Payout = ₹1,20,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹1,10,000. The same claim cannot be paid twice because its hash is already on the ledger.
chapters.trap: Double-counting the deductible or assuming a blockchain can check medical necessity; it checks data and rules, not the truth of off-chain events without an oracle.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 smart contracts; Unit 2 digital signatures.
chapters.leave: Bitcoin payments and insurance law to Unit 4 and a law course.

chapters.idea: A supply chain ledger records each custody change and quantity as a hash-linked event, so any later edit breaks the chain and exposes the gap.
chapters.depth: Cover provenance, chain of custody, batch and lot IDs, temperature and cold chain, customs documents, ERP integration, logistics handovers, recalls. Explain on-chain hash plus off-chain document. Mention smart contracts for payment on delivery. Some syllabi call this 'supply chain insight from ERP'.

figure.title: Chain of custody for batch B001
figure.aria: Farm records 100 kg, transporter records 98 kg, warehouse records 98 kg, and retailer records 95 kg, with hash pointers linking the events.
figure.caption: Each event is linked to the previous one, so the 2 kg and 3 kg losses are visible at the handovers.

chapters.example: Batch B001 of mangoes starts with 100 kg at the farm. The transporter records 98 kg, the warehouse records 98 kg, and the retailer records 95 kg. The ledger shows a 2 kg loss between farm and transporter and a 3 kg loss between warehouse and retailer. Total recorded loss = 100 − 95 = 5 kg. The 2 kg and 3 kg events are the points to audit.
chapters.trap: Believing a blockchain weighs the goods; the weight is an input, and the ledger only proves the record was not changed later.
chapters.leave: Consensus details and ERP coding to Unit 3 and an ERP course.

chapters.idea: Health, agriculture, IoT and smart-city systems use the same pattern: devices or organisations write signed data to a shared ledger, and applications read a verifiable history.
chapters.depth: Cover health records and consent, clinical trials, pharma cold chain; agri provenance and payments; IoT device identity and firmware logs; smart-city parking, energy, waste, e-governance; smart grid. Explain off-chain storage and Merkle roots. Some syllabi split smart grid and e-governance into separate case studies.

figure.title: Vaccine cold chain with an IoT ledger
figure.aria: A vaccine fridge sends signed readings through an IoT gateway, the blockchain stores a Merkle root, a health app raises an alert, and an auditor verifies one reading.
figure.caption: The ledger stores a root, not every raw reading; the auditor verifies a reading with a short Merkle proof.

chapters.example: A vaccine fridge sends one temperature reading every 10 minutes, so 6 × 24 = 144 readings per day. Three readings are above 8 °C. The gateway stores all 144 readings off-chain and writes one Merkle root on-chain. To prove one reading to an auditor, the Merkle proof needs about log₂ 144 ≈ 8 hashes. The auditor checks the root and the 8 hashes, not all 144 readings.
chapters.trap: Putting raw IoT data on-chain; store a hash or root off-chain and keep the chain small.
chapters.leave: IoT networking, consensus and machine learning to other courses.

chapters.idea: The metaverse is a set of immersive digital experiences built on a seven-layer value chain, and blockchains provide ownership, identity and payments for its virtual assets.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover definition, immersive experience (VR and AR), history from text worlds to 3D worlds, and the 7-layer value chain: Experience, Discovery, Creator Economy, Spatial Computing, Decentralization, Human Interface, Infrastructure. Explain NFTs, virtual land, wallets, payments and identity. Avoid claiming exact dates.

figure.aria: Seven metaverse layers from Experience at the top through Discovery, Creator Economy, Spatial Computing, Decentralization and Human Interface down to Infrastructure.
figure.caption: The blockchain layer is one part of the metaverse value chain, not the whole metaverse.

chapters.example: A user buys virtual land for 2 ETH. The platform fee is 2.5%. Fee = 2 × 0.025 = 0.05 ETH. Seller receives 2 − 0.05 = 1.95 ETH. The land NFT moves to the buyer's wallet, and the ledger records the sale; the 3D scene itself is stored off-chain.
chapters.trap: Treating the metaverse as only VR or only blockchain; the value chain has experience and infrastructure layers too.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 tokens and smart contracts; Chapter 6.2 chaincode.
chapters.leave: 3D graphics and NFT standard details to specialised chapters.

chapters.idea: Ripple, Quorum, Tendermint, Kadena and Rootstock are different answers to settlement, privacy, BFT finality, scalability and Bitcoin compatibility.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover Ripple and the XRP Ledger for payments and validators; Quorum as private or permissioned Ethereum; Tendermint BFT and Cosmos; Kadena Chainweb braid and Pact; Rootstock as a Bitcoin sidechain with EVM. Compare consensus, permissioning, token and finality. Some syllabi list Rootstock with side chains.

figure.aria: A root labelled Platforms branches to Ripple for payments, Quorum for private EVM, Tendermint for BFT finality, Kadena for braided chains, and Rootstock for Bitcoin compatibility.
figure.caption: Each platform is a different design choice, not a simple upgrade of the others.

chapters.example: A Tendermint network has 7 validators. The Byzantine fault tolerance is f = floor((n − 1) / 3) = floor(6/3) = 2. A quorum is 2f + 1 = 5 validators. With 5 votes the block can commit; with 4 votes it cannot.
chapters.trap: Mixing up Tendermint's BFT quorum with Bitcoin's longest-chain rule; they give different finality.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 consensus; Unit 5 EVM and smart contracts.
chapters.leave: Full consensus proofs and token economics to Unit 3 and advanced courses.

chapters.idea: Blockchains trade throughput, latency, storage, privacy and decentralisation against each other, and no single design removes all limits.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover the scalability trilemma, TPS, block size, block interval, storage growth, layer 1 versus layer 2, sharding, rollups, channels, private data, zero-knowledge proofs, regulatory and energy issues, interoperability and quantum risk. Some syllabi call this 'scalability, privacy and other challenges'.

figure.aria: A triangle with Decentralisation, Security and Scalability at its corners, joined by trade-off edges for validators, throughput and cost.
figure.caption: Improving one corner usually puts pressure on another; the triangle is a design trade-off, not a strict law.

chapters.example: A chain makes blocks every 12 s. Each block holds 1,000 transactions, and each transaction record is 500 bytes. Throughput = 1,000 / 12 ≈ 83.3 tx/s. Blocks per day = 86,400 / 12 = 7,200. Daily ledger data = 7,200 × 1,000 × 500 B = 3,600,000,000 B = 3.6 GB/day.
chapters.trap: Using TPS alone; storage and privacy can block a design even when TPS looks high.
chapters.leave: Detailed cryptography and PoW mining to Unit 2 and Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Enterprise blockchains add permissioning, identity and integration to shared ledgers, and AI adds prediction and model audit on top of that trusted data.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover consortium networks, Blockchain as a Service, ERP integration, oracles, on-chain versus off-chain data, AI for fraud and forecasting, model provenance, federated learning and audit trails. Some syllabi call this 'next generation blockchain enterprise AI'.

figure.aria: An enterprise logs an input hash on the blockchain, the AI service reads approved data and stores a model hash, the enterprise gets a prediction, and an auditor verifies the model hash.
figure.caption: The ledger anchors hashes of inputs and models; the raw data and the model itself stay off-chain.

chapters.example: An enterprise logs 1,000 AI predictions per day. Each log stores a 32-byte input hash and a 32-byte model hash. Storage per day = 1,000 × (32 + 32) B = 64,000 B = 64 kB. For 30 days = 64 kB × 30 = 1,920 kB ≈ 1.92 MB. The raw inputs and model stay off-chain.
chapters.trap: Storing full training data or models on-chain; store hashes and pointers, keep private data off-chain.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.2 chaincode; Chapter 6.8 limits; Chapter 6.5 IoT data.
chapters.leave: Machine-learning algorithms and consensus details to other courses.
